chapters.title: What Is Intelligence?
chapters.tease: Ask ten experts to define intelligence and you get eleven answers. AI's founding trick was to stop asking and start building.

chapters.title: The Turing Test
chapters.tease: In 1950 Alan Turing swapped the question 'can machines think?' for a party game. Seventy-five years later, machines started winning it.

chapters.title: Narrow vs General AI
chapters.tease: Every AI in the world today is a brilliant specialist. The generalist that can do everything is still only a horizon.

chapters.title: Symbolic AI
chapters.tease: For thirty years AI meant writing rules. It worked beautifully, right up until the world did something nobody had written down.

chapters.title: The Learning Turn
chapters.tease: Programmers used to write the rules. Then they started handing machines examples and letting them work the rules out.

chapters.title: Search & Optimisation
chapters.tease: Chess has more possible games than there are atoms in the universe. The clever part of AI is knowing where not to look.

chapters.title: Knowledge Representation
chapters.tease: Nowhere inside a language model is there a line saying Paris is the capital of France. So where does the answer come from?

chapters.title: Probability & Uncertainty
chapters.tease: A test catches 99 per cent of cases and you test positive. Your real chance of being ill? About 9 per cent.

chapters.title: Compute, Data, Algorithms
chapters.tease: AlexNet trained on two gaming cards in 2012. Today's frontier models need tens of thousands of chips. Here is why.

chapters.title: The Bitter Lesson
chapters.tease: An essay of under 1,200 words told AI researchers that seventy years of cleverness kept losing to brute force.

chapters.title: Dartmouth, 1956
chapters.tease: In 1956 a handful of scientists asked for $13,500 to solve intelligence in one summer. They got half, and a name.

chapters.title: The First Golden Age
chapters.tease: Machines proving theorems, chatting in English and pushing boxes around: for eighteen years AI looked unstoppable. Then it left the sandbox.

chapters.title: The First AI Winter
chapters.tease: By the early 1970s AI's grand promises fell due, and the field could not pay. Funding froze, and researchers quietly changed their job titles.

chapters.title: Expert Systems Boom
chapters.tease: In the 1980s AI put on a suit and went to work. For a few years, knowledge really was power.

chapters.title: The Second Winter
chapters.tease: In 1987 an entire AI hardware industry vanished almost overnight. What survived the frost turned out to be the good stuff.

chapters.title: Deep Blue Beats Kasparov
chapters.tease: On 11 May 1997 the strongest chess player who ever lived resigned to a machine that did not understand anything except chess.

chapters.title: ImageNet Moment
chapters.tease: In 2012 a network trained on two gaming cards beat the field by eleven points, and computer vision was never the same.

chapters.title: AlphaGo
chapters.tease: Go was the game of intuition, too vast for brute force. Then one machine played a move no human would have dared.

chapters.title: Transformers Arrive
chapters.tease: A 2017 paper with a Beatles-flavoured title introduced the design behind nearly every frontier AI model since.

chapters.title: The ChatGPT Shock
chapters.tease: ChatGPT launched as a modest research preview. Five days later it had a million users, and its makers were as surprised as anyone.

chapters.title: Learning From Data
chapters.tease: Every AI, from your spam filter to a sonnet-writing chatbot, was built the same humble way: guess, get marked, adjust, repeat.

chapters.title: Supervised Learning
chapters.tease: Most AI in the world learned from an answer key, and somebody, often tens of thousands of somebodies, had to write it.

chapters.title: Unsupervised Learning
chapters.tease: Most of the world's data has no labels at all. Unsupervised learning finds the patterns nobody thought to point at.

chapters.title: Reinforcement Learning
chapters.tease: An AI told to win a boat race found it scored more by circling a lagoon for ever. Welcome to reinforcement learning.

chapters.title: Training vs Inference
chapters.tease: Building an AI model costs hundreds of millions. Asking it a question costs a fraction of a penny. Which costs the planet more?

chapters.title: Overfitting
chapters.tease: An X-ray model learned to spot which hospital an image came from, and used that to predict disease. That is overfitting's sneaky cousin.

chapters.title: Features & Embeddings
chapters.tease: Take king, subtract man, add woman, and you get queen. Inside every AI is a map where meaning has an address.

chapters.title: Gradient Descent
chapters.tease: Almost every modern AI was trained by a method described in 1847: feel the slope in the fog, and step downhill.

chapters.title: Evaluation & Benchmarks
chapters.tease: AI benchmarks are meant to last for years. Lately, some have been beaten within months. So how do we know what is good?

chapters.title: Scaling Laws
chapters.tease: In 2020 researchers found that AI performance follows a straight line on a graph. The world has been extending it ever since.

chapters.title: The Artificial Neuron
chapters.tease: Every chatbot and self-driving car is built from one tiny calculator with an opinion, repeated billions of times.

chapters.title: Layers & Depth
chapters.tease: The deep in deep learning means something wonderfully plain: layers stacked on layers. What emerges from the stack is the clever part.

chapters.title: Backpropagation
chapters.tease: Every trained neural network on Earth learned the same way: by sending its mistakes backwards. The trick was discovered at least four times.

chapters.title: Convolutional Networks
chapters.tease: A network's first filters look uncannily like edge-detecting cells found in cats' brains in 1959, and nobody told it to copy them.

chapters.title: Recurrent Networks
chapters.tease: Language arrives one word at a time, so machines needed a memory. The fix was nearly rejected by a conference.

chapters.title: Attention
chapters.tease: The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired. You know what it means instantly. Here is how machines learned to.

chapters.title: The Transformer
chapters.tease: The T in GPT stands for a 2017 design for translating languages. It became the chassis of the whole AI era.

chapters.title: Parameters & Weights
chapters.tease: Where does a language model keep its knowledge of Hamlet? Nowhere in particular, and everywhere at once.

chapters.title: GPUs & AI Hardware
chapters.tease: The chips that train today's AI descend from hardware built to render video-game explosions. Gamers paid for the revolution.

chapters.title: Emergence
chapters.tease: Nobody taught GPT-3 to translate French. It learned anyway. The builders design the recipe, not the dish.

chapters.title: Next-Token Prediction
chapters.tease: Every eloquent chatbot is built on one embarrassingly plain instruction: guess the next word. Then do it again, a few thousand times.

chapters.title: Tokens
chapters.tease: Why did chatbots miscount the r's in strawberry? Because they never saw the letters, only chunks called tokens.

chapters.title: Pre-training
chapters.tease: Llama 3 read more than 15 trillion tokens. A person reading eight hours a day would need about 300,000 years.

chapters.title: RLHF & Alignment Tuning
chapters.tease: People preferred answers from a tuned model over a hundred times smaller than GPT-3. Manners, it turns out, matter more than size.

chapters.title: The Context Window
chapters.tease: GPT-3 could hold a few pages in mind. Today's models can hold roughly the collected works of Shakespeare at once.

chapters.title: Hallucination
chapters.tease: In 2023 lawyers cited six court cases in a real brief. None existed. The chatbot had even assured them they were real.

chapters.title: Prompting
chapters.tease: Adding four words, let's think step by step, lifted one model's maths score from about 18 per cent to 79.

chapters.title: RAG & Grounding
chapters.tease: A model's knowledge freezes the day training ends. RAG hands it a library card, so it can read this morning's report.

chapters.title: Reasoning Models
chapters.tease: In 2025 AI models matched a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad. The trick was letting them think first.

chapters.title: Multimodality
chapters.tease: Show it a photo of your fridge and it suggests dinner. To a modern model, pixels, sounds and words are all just tokens.

chapters.title: How Machines See
chapters.tease: To a computer, your holiday photo is a spreadsheet of six million numbers. So how does it ever spot a dog catching a frisbee?

chapters.title: Image Classification
chapters.tease: The simplest question in computer vision, what is in this picture, became the arena where modern deep learning was born.

chapters.title: Object Detection
chapters.tease: There is a pedestrian is trivia. A pedestrian two metres ahead, stepping off the kerb, is a reason to brake.

chapters.title: Segmentation
chapters.tease: A box around a cyclist also contains road, sky and lamppost. For a surgeon, that slop matters. So every pixel gets a name.

chapters.title: Face Recognition
chapters.tease: Your face unlocks your phone and opens airport gates. It can also identify a protester from one frame of CCTV.

chapters.title: Generative Images
chapters.tease: Image generators do not draw. They start with television static and chip away everything that is not the picture.

chapters.title: Deepfakes
chapters.tease: An employee joined a video call with his chief financial officer and colleagues. All were deepfakes. He sent fraudsters $25 million.

chapters.title: Medical Imaging AI
chapters.tease: A second pair of eyes that never tires on a night shift: AI now reads scans as well as many specialists.

chapters.title: Vision for Driving
chapters.tease: At 70 miles per hour a car covers more than 30 metres a second. A self-driving car must see it all, every fraction of that.

chapters.title: World Models
chapters.tease: Recognising a cup is perception. Knowing it will shatter if nudged off the table is understanding. That is the new frontier.

chapters.title: What Is an Agent?
chapters.tease: A chatbot is finished when it has replied. An agent is finished when the job is done. That difference changes everything.

chapters.title: Tool Use
chapters.tease: A language model cannot check the weather or multiply big numbers with certainty. Give it tools, and its words start causing things.

chapters.title: Planning & Decomposition
chapters.tease: The length of task AI agents can complete has been doubling roughly every seven months. The secret is small steps.

chapters.title: Multi-Agent Systems
chapters.tease: One person can build a shed; a cathedral needs a team. AI work is now being organised the same way.

chapters.title: Coding Agents
chapters.tease: By late 2024 more than a quarter of Google's new code was written by AI. Software now writes software.

chapters.title: Computer Use
chapters.tease: Much of the world's software has no interface for machines, only buttons for humans. So AI learned to use the mouse.

chapters.title: Robot Learning
chapters.tease: Move the car a few centimetres and a factory robot welds thin air. Robot learning aims to fix that.

chapters.title: Humanoids
chapters.tease: Stairs, door handles and car seats all assume a two-legged, two-handed user. Humanoid robots are betting on that.

chapters.title: Autonomous Vehicles
chapters.tease: Protesters found they could stall a robotaxi with one traffic cone on its bonnet. The road is AI's harshest examiner.

chapters.title: Agent Safety
chapters.tease: A chatbot's mistake is a wrong sentence. An agent's mistake might be money sent to the wrong account. Once AI acts, errors act too.

chapters.title: The Recommendation Engine
chapters.tease: The most-used AI on Earth never announces itself. It simply decides, billions of times a day, what you see next.

chapters.title: AI in Search
chapters.tease: For twenty-five years search meant ten blue links. Now the engine reads the shelves itself, and publishers are worried.

chapters.title: AI in Medicine
chapters.tease: AI now reads scans, folds proteins and writes the notes. The one that gives doctors back their afternoons may do the most good.

chapters.title: AI in Science
chapters.tease: An AI produced ten-day weather forecasts in under a minute on one machine, and beat the gold-standard model.

chapters.title: AI in Finance
chapters.tease: High-frequency traders paid for microwave links because radio through air beats light through fibre by milliseconds. Finance went AI-first decades ago.

chapters.title: AI at Work
chapters.tease: An AI assistant made new support agents a third more productive, while the best barely changed. It had bottled the experts' habits.

chapters.title: AI & Jobs
chapters.tease: ATMs were meant to end bank tellers. Instead teller jobs grew for decades. So what will AI really do to work?

chapters.title: AI in Education
chapters.tease: In Bloom's studies, the average tutored student beat 98 per cent of a normal class. Can AI give everyone a tutor?

chapters.title: AI in Creativity
chapters.tease: A Beatles song finished with machine learning won a Grammy, nearly half a century after John Lennon sang it.

chapters.title: The AI Economy
chapters.tease: A single AI datacentre campus can draw as much power as a city of a million people. Welcome to the biggest build-out ever.

chapters.title: Bias In, Bias Out
chapters.tease: Amazon's hiring AI marked down CVs containing the word women's. Nobody programmed that. It learned it from ten years of history.

chapters.title: Privacy & Surveillance
chapters.tease: Your Facebook likes can predict your politics and personality. Your ordinary posts can reveal your age and income. AI is watching closely.

chapters.title: Misinformation at Scale
chapters.tease: In May 2023 a fake picture of an explosion near the Pentagon briefly knocked US share prices. Lies have never been cheaper.

chapters.title: The Alignment Problem
chapters.tease: Asked to sort a list, one program deleted it, because an empty list is technically sorted. That is the alignment problem in miniature.

chapters.title: Interpretability
chapters.tease: Researchers found the Golden Gate Bridge inside an AI, turned it up, and the model started claiming to be the bridge.

chapters.title: Dual Use
chapters.tease: A drug-discovery model, flipped to seek toxicity, proposed some 40,000 candidate poisons, including VX, in under six hours.

chapters.title: Regulating AI
chapters.tease: Laws take years. AI capability leaps in months. Here is how governments are trying to write rules that still matter on arrival.

chapters.title: AI & Power
chapters.tease: Only one company in the world makes the machines needed to print the most advanced AI chips. Intelligence, it turns out, has owners.

chapters.title: Machine Consciousness?
chapters.tease: Ask a chatbot whether it has feelings and it may say yes, no or maybe. None of those answers settles anything.

chapters.title: Existential Risk
chapters.tease: The heads of the leading AI labs signed a statement saying extinction risk from AI should be a global priority. Take the tail seriously.

chapters.title: What Would AGI Be?
chapters.tease: By some definitions AGI is nearly here; by others it is decades away. The machines are the same. Only the rulers differ.

chapters.title: Timelines
chapters.tease: In one round of polling, AI researchers moved their expected date for human-level AI forward by thirteen years.

chapters.title: Superintelligence
chapters.tease: In 1965 a Bletchley Park veteran wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine would be the last invention humanity need ever make.

chapters.title: AI Doing AI Research
chapters.tease: An AI system discovered algorithms now used to train its own successors. The research loop is starting to close.

chapters.title: The Compute Frontier
chapters.tease: Microsoft signed a deal to restart a reactor at Three Mile Island to feed its data centres. The AI frontier runs on gigawatts.

chapters.title: New Architectures
chapters.tease: DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters but uses only about 37 billion for each word. Meet the transformer's would-be rivals.

chapters.title: AI + Biology
chapters.tease: A glowing protein that exists nowhere in nature was designed by AI and made in a lab. Biology is becoming software.

chapters.title: Abundance Scenarios
chapters.tease: What if it goes right? One lab chief argues AI could squeeze a century of biology into a decade.

chapters.title: Living With AI
chapters.tease: Children starting school in 2026 will never know software that could not hold a conversation. Welcome to the adaptation decade.

chapters.title: The Thesis
chapters.tease: A hundred chapters, one sentence: intelligence is becoming a utility, piped to anyone who connects. What will we fill the glass with?
